result.source_concept: CLI tool output design (unformatted text vs structured JSON and flags)

mappings.source_element: Unformatted text printed to the console
mappings.evidence: Analogy states the unformatted text is only useful to a human who can read it directly, likening it to a product without accessibility.

mappings.source_element: Structured JSON output and clear command-line flags
mappings.target_element: Inclusive design and assistive technologies (e.g., screen readers)
mappings.relation: provides a machine‑readable interface analogous to inclusive design that enables assistive technologies to interpret and interact
mappings.evidence: Analogy describes redesigning the tool to output structured JSON and flags as creating a machine‑readable API (inclusive design) for scripts (assistive technologies).

mappings.source_element: Automated scripts that parse the JSON
mappings.target_element: People with diverse abilities using assistive technologies
mappings.relation: acts as the consumer of the accessible interface
mappings.evidence: Analogy says scripts can reliably parse the output, understand the data, and interact, making it useful for a new set of automated consumers (people with diverse abilities).

result.process_summary: Both the CLI redesign and accessibility improvements involve transforming a raw, human‑only output into a structured, machine‑readable format. This transformation creates a stable interface that external agents—automated scripts in the CLI case, assistive technologies in the accessibility case—can reliably parse, interpret, and act upon, thereby extending usability to a broader set of users.
potential_breaks: Scripts are not equivalent to human users; the analogy may over‑simplify the cognitive and sensory differences between automated parsers and people with disabilities.

The mapping of command‑line flags to assistive‑technology features is imperfect; flags aid programmatic control, whereas assistive tech often requires semantic labeling, contrast, and navigation cues beyond mere data format.
Assuming all assistive technologies can consume JSON ignores the diversity of assistive tools (e.g., screen readers that rely on HTML semantics rather than raw JSON).
